newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain convicts ex-spy of stealing top secret files.
newsitem.headline: Spain convicts ex-spy of stealing top secret files.

text.p: Spain's former head of covert operations was convicted on Thursday of stealing secret files which helped lead to the downfall of the Socialist government last year.

Spain's central military court sentenced Colonel Juan Alberto Perote to seven years in prison for stealing the top secret files, including some vital to state security and others that implicated the former Socialist government in a "dirty war" against Basque separatists in the 1980s.
Stripped of the right to wear his military uniform for the sentencing, Perote emerged from the courtroom in civilian attire and appeared relieved by the verdict.
"The sentence was much better than I expected," he told reporters. Prosecutors had asked he be sentenced to 10 years.
The former secret service number two was found to have stolen 1,200 documents from Spain's military intelligence department CESID when he was sacked in 1991.
Prosecutors said he later peddled the documents to newspapers, businessmen and parties interested in undermining the Socialists.
In his defence, Perote, who has already spent more than 21 months in jail awaiting trial, maintained that he had not deliberately stolen the files. His lawyer said he would appeal.
Perote headed CESID's Operative Group, which handled the Defence Ministry's most sensitive security cases, for nine years.
The files he was found to have taken record briefings Perote held with his boss, CESID head Lieutenant-General Emilio Alonso Manglano, on clandestine operations.

The anti-Socialist newspaper El Mundo in 1995 published files which appeared to show that former prime minister Felipe Gonzalez and his associates set up undercover squads to combat separatist violence by ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom). The squads killed 28 people between 1983 and 1987.

Although it is has not been established that these files were genuine, the scandal that broke when they were published led to a raft of resignations including those of a deputy prime minister, the defence minister and Manglano.
They also tainted the Socialists in the eyes of the Spanish public and contributed to their election defeat in March 1996 after more than 13 years in power.

Socialist Party leader Joaquin Almunia welcomed the court verdict. "The sentence was deserved...and hopefully this will never happen again in Spain, especially in the intelligence service," he told reporters.

Perote is believed to have microfilmed the documents and destroyed a large number of the originals six months before he was fired. Officials say he eventually returned the files, although it is not clear whether he handed back originals or legally worthless copies.
He was arrested in June 1995 after El Mundo published its excerpts.

Copies of the files were later found during a court search of Perote's prison cell. In a desperate attempt to destroy the evidence he crammed some of the papers in his mouth and tried to swallow them, jugdes said.
The papers have remained classified by request of the previous Socialist government and the current conservative administration, who argue they contain state secrets.

But judges investigating the "dirty war" say the documents contain vital evidence against senior Socialists, including Gonzalez, and in April the Supreme Court overturned a previous decision and ordered the government to declassify 13 of the files.
